headline: Man Haunted by Fear That Every 'You Too' to 'Enjoy Your Meal' Was Recorded
subheadline: Anxiety about awkward responses prompts investigation into restaurant surveillance
summary: A man's paranoia about his social mistakes has led to a surprisingly serious investigation of restaurant camera practices.
content:
Local man Jeremy Okonkwo has spent the past three months investigating restaurant surveillance practices, driven by the persistent fear that every time he said "you too" after a server said "enjoy your meal," it was recorded.

"It happened again last Tuesday," Okonkwo explained. "Server says 'enjoy your meal,' my brain says 'say thank you,' my mouth says 'you too,' and now that exchange exists forever on some security camera somewhere. That's evidence. Evidence of my failure."

Okonkwo's investigation began after he calculated he had committed this specific social error approximately 847 times in his adult life. "That's 847 recordings of me telling someone who isn't eating to enjoy their meal," he said. "Where do those recordings go? Who reviews them? Are they laughing?"

His research has revealed that most restaurant security footage is automatically deleted after 30-90 days, which provided temporary relief. However, Okonkwo then became concerned about the instances that might have been preserved.

"What if one of my 'you too's happened during an incident that required footage to be saved?" he asked. "What if my awkward moment is now evidence in some unrelated case? What if a detective is watching me say 'you too' right now?"

The investigation has expanded to include interactions with flight attendants ("Have a nice flight!" "You too!—wait, you're staying on the plane"), movie theater workers ("Enjoy the show!" "You too!—you're not watching it"), and one memorable encounter with a hearse driver.

"He said 'Sorry for your loss.' I said 'You too.' That one haunts me more than the others."

Okonkwo has since developed coping strategies, including rehearsing appropriate responses and "accepting that everyone does this and most people don't remember."

"But the cameras remember," he added. "The cameras always remember."
author: Chris Patterson, Human Interest
